extracted.intended_audience: Catholic faithful / catechism students (general readers preparing in religious instruction)
extracted.subtask_description: A catechetical exposition of the moral rules embodied in the Ten Commandments with practical guidance, examples, exceptions, and duties (oaths, vows, Sunday observance, duties to parents, theft, false witness, etc.). Intended to teach proper observance and moral reasoning to learners of Catholic doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lawful oath requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: To make an oath lawful it is necessary that what we swear be true, and that there be a sufficient cause for taking an oath.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges, magistrates, officers take oaths because a lie in testimony can have grave consequences; an oath should be taken only when truth is intended and there is sufficient reason. False, rash, unjust, or unnecessary oaths are forbidden (see Second Commandment guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Valid vow conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: A vow is a deliberate promise made to God to do something that is pleasing to Him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "Deliberate" means with full consent and freedom (forced vows are invalid). A vow must be made to God (not merely to another) and must be for something pleasing to God; a promise to do something forbidden by God is not a valid vow and keeping such a vow would be sinful. Example: King Herod's rash vow to grant whatever was asked (Matt. 14) was not binding in conscience because it was not something pleasing to God.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forbidden membership in certain secret societies
rubrics_metrics.description: Catholics commit sin by joining secret societies that require unconditional obedience or expose members to being forced to sin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Church forbids joining societies whose objects are unlawful, whose means used are sinful, or which violate conscience and liberty by rash or dangerous oaths. Such societies may undermine Church authority and even recommend assassination; lawful associations founded on law and justice (e.g., legitimate labor unions, benefit societies) are not secret societies simply because they meet in private.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sinfulness of not fulfilling lawful vows
rubrics_metrics.description: Not to fulfill lawful vows is a sin, either mortal or venial according to the nature of the vow and the intention when making it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The gravity of failing to keep a vow depends on the vow itself and the promisor's intention at the time of making it. A person who intends only a venial obligation when taking a pledge will incur venial sin for breaking it, unless they intended to bind themselves under mortal sin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second Commandment prohibitions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Second Commandment forbids all false, rash, unjust, and unnecessary oaths, blasphemy, cursing, and profane words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "Rash" means swearing truth or falsehood without knowing for certain. "Blasphemy" is more serious than cursing: it is saying or doing something very disrespectful to God (e.g., defying God by sign or action). "Profane words" are irreverent and irreligious words. Example given: Julian the Apostate's acts and words as an example of blasphemy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third Commandment: keep the Lord's Day holy
rubrics_metrics.description: The Third Commandment commands keeping holy the Lord's Day and holy days of obligation by giving time to the service and worship of God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observance normally includes hearing Mass and refraining from servile works; there must be a good reason to work on a holy day. Beyond the bare obligation, those who love God should do more: restful but not vulgar entertainments, pious reading, charity, visiting the Blessed Sacrament, attending devotions. Avoid spending the whole day in worthless reading or idle pursuits; have good Catholic newspapers and standard books (e.g., New Testament, Imitation of Christ, a full catechism). Not all celebratory days are holy days of obligation (examples: St. Patrick's Day, Corpus Christi may not be obligations in all places).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between Sabbath and Sunday
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sabbath (seventh day) and Sunday (first day) are not the same: Sunday is kept holy in the New Law because Christ rose and sent the Holy Ghost on Sunday.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keeping Sunday instead of the Jewish Sabbath teaches that the Old Law is replaced by the New Law of Christ. This underpins Sunday worship and its obligations in Christian practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of unnecessary servile work on holy days
rubrics_metrics.description: The Third Commandment forbids all unnecessary servile work and whatever else hinders due observance of the Lord's day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Servile works are those requiring bodily rather than mental labor. Work is permitted when required by the honor of God, the good of our neighbor, or necessity (examples: erecting an altar that cannot be built at another time; repairing a bridge; attending to fire or ship duties).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and exceptions for servile works
rubrics_metrics.description: Servile works are those which require labor rather of body than of mind (work of slaves); writing, reading, studying are not servile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Servile works are lawful on Sunday when required for the honor of God, the good of neighbor, or necessity. Examples: erecting an altar, clearing obstacles after an accident, firemen extinguishing fires, sailors working at sea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fourth Commandment duties to parents
rubrics_metrics.description: The Fourth Commandment: Honor thy father and thy mother — to honor, love, and obey parents in all that is not sin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obedience excludes commands that are certainly sinful; if forced to sin by superiors, the blame lies with them. Help and support parents when needed; do not despise parents for lack of culture or refinement; do not waste parents' sacrifices by idleness. Examples and moral exhortation: reflect on duties, ask 'What good am I doing here?', emulate saints' conscientiousness about time and action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to honor other lawful superiors
rubrics_metrics.description: We are bound to honor and obey bishops, pastors, magistrates, teachers, and other lawful superiors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "Magistrates" include civil rulers like president, governor, mayor, judges, etc. Respect for lawful authority is required within moral limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties of parents and superiors toward those under charge
rubrics_metrics.description: Parents and superiors must take good care of all under their charge and give proper direction and example.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This duty is so important that God will hold them responsible for neglect; parents act as God's agents and may justly punish children for their good. Good example leads to good results across generations; bad example can propagate vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fourth Commandment prohibitions (disobedience, contempt, stubbornness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Fourth Commandment forbids all disobedience, contempt, and stubbornness towards our parents or lawful superiors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "Contempt" is showing by words or actions that we despise those placed over us (e.g., contempt of court). "Stubbornness" is sulky, unwilling obedience even when wrong. Acts normally venial may become mortal if done out of contempt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fifth Commandment obligations (respect for life)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Fifth Commandment: Thou shalt not kill — commands us to live in peace and union with our neighbor, to respect his rights, seek his spiritual and bodily welfare, and to take proper care of our own life and health.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Our life is lent by God; suicide is a mortal sin when done in sound mind. It is sinful to risk life uselessly or continue habits that harm health. Habitual drunkenness and disobedient harmful habits (e.g., minors smoking against parents' orders) are violations because they injure health and hasten death.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fifth Commandment prohibitions (murder, anger, revenge)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Fifth Commandment forbids all willful murder, fighting, anger, hatred, revenge, and bad example.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It forbids anything that might lead to murder; revenge is the desire to injure others because they injured you. Bad example that leads others toward violence is also forbidden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sixth Commandment obligations (purity and modesty)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sixth Commandment: Thou shalt not commit adultery — commands us to be pure in thought and modest in looks, words, and actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violations of the Sixth are frequently mortal sins. Guard all senses (eyes, ears, tongue) because temptations enter through the senses; do not leave any 'door' unguarded. Vigilance is required because temptation through the senses is pervasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sixth Commandment prohibitions (unchastity and immodesty)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sixth Commandment forbids all unchaste freedom with another's wife or husband and all immodesty in looks, dress, words, or actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes prohibiting immodest behavior with oneself or others; sexual fidelity and chastity are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on reading bad or immodest books (Sixth Commandment application)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sixth Commandment forbids the reading of bad and immodest books and newspapers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reading connects the reader to the author; bad books can make deeper impressions than speech because they can be reread and dwelt upon. Avoid 'trashy' or suggestive works that corrupt virtue. Prefer good story-books by good authors, and consult pastors, teachers, parents about reading choices. Avoid wasting mental capacity on nonsense; fill mind with true knowledge and good literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seventh Commandment admonition against stealing
rubrics_metrics.description: The Seventh Commandment: Thou shalt not steal — commands honesty; even small dishonest acts (a nut, cake, cent) are stealing and can lead to a life of dishonesty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many forms of violating the commandment: workers not doing a just day's work, employers cheating wages, merchants charging unjust prices, giving light weight or short measure, misrepresenting goods, speculation or gambling with others' money, borrowing without intent to repay, not paying just debts, purchasing knowing you cannot pay. Small daily thefts accumulate into grave sin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seventh Commandment duty to respect property
rubrics_metrics.description: By the Seventh Commandment we are commanded to give to all men what belongs to them and to respect their property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respecting property means acknowledging others' rights and doing nothing to violate those rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seventh Commandment prohibitions (unjust taking/keeping and complicity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Seventh Commandment forbids all unjust taking or keeping what belongs to another and includes sharing in another's sin by receiving stolen goods or aiding theft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guilty by receiving stolen goods knowingly; guilty by ordering, advising, praising, consenting to wrong when one should oppose it; guilty by protecting wrongdoers or neglecting to prevent theft when duty (e.g., paid guard). If one unknowingly buys stolen goods, one must restore them when owner claims them; if you find something you must sincerely seek the owner and return it; if owner cannot be found after sincere search you may keep it, but if delay made restoration impossible you must give value to rightful heirs or to the poor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to restore ill-gotten goods and make reparations
rubrics_metrics.description: We are bound to restore ill-gotten goods, or the value of them, as far as we are able; otherwise we cannot be forgiven.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "Ill-gotten" means unjustly obtained. If the stolen article is lost or destroyed, give the owner its value. Restoration need not include an admission of theft to the owner unless the owner already knew; restoration must be prompt—delaying restitution after being able to restore risks sacrilege in receiving the sacraments without proper disposition. If one cannot restore immediately, a firm resolution to restore as soon as possible is necessary for absolution; intention suffices until means are available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to repair unjustly caused damage
rubrics_metrics.description: We are bound to repair the damage we have unjustly caused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restitution and repair of damage are moral obligations in addition to returning stolen goods; one must make good whatever injury one has caused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eighth Commandment obligations (truth and reputation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Eighth Commandment: Thou shalt not bear false witness — commands us to speak the truth in all things and to be careful of the honor and reputation of everyone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reputation is a good that once taken cannot be fully restored; injuring a person's good name is morally grave, often worse than stealing money. Only necessary exposures for the good of the person or others excuse speaking of faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of offenses against reputation and required reparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Detraction is exposing someone's real faults; calumny is accusing of faults not committed; slander is malicious circulation of damaging reports. All injure reputation and require repair.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you have told lies about someone, you must acknowledge to those you spoke with that you were untrue and compensate for losses (e.g., loss of job). If what you said was true, you should at every opportunity say whatever good you can of the person before those you misled. Reparation includes restoring reputation where possible and making amends for harm done.
